sections.title: 1. What habeas corpus does
sections.subtitle: Ask the government to justify custody.

parts.title: Start with the person
parts.text: A detained person’s first questions are often practical: Where am I? Why am I being held? Can someone help me challenge it? Habeas corpus is a judicial process for testing the legal basis for custody. The petition asks a court with authority over the case to examine detention and grant an appropriate remedy if the law requires one. It is a way to demand a lawful explanation and judicial review, not a promise that every detention ends. An advocate begins by listening, preserving the record, and connecting the person to qualified counsel.

parts.title: The constitutional foundation
parts.text: The Suspension Clause protects the privilege of the writ and specifies the exceptional conditions under which suspension may occur. Modern federal habeas authority also depends on statutes and precedent. The constitutional protection does not erase the rules governing custody, the right court, procedural requirements, or the claim being presented. The Latin phrase is commonly rendered “you have the body”; today the meaningful question is whether the government has lawful authority to restrain this person.

parts.title: Petition, writ, remedy
parts.text: A petition is the request initiating the case. The court may order a response, evaluate facts and legal arguments, and deny or grant relief. A favorable decision may require release, a legally adequate custody hearing, or another tailored remedy. Winning access to a hearing is different from winning release; winning release from detention is different from winning an immigration status or defeating removal. Keep the requested remedy tied to the legal defect.

questions.prompt: What is the central habeas question?
options: Will a passport be issued?
Is this custody lawful under the applicable law?
Which immigration benefit will be approved?
questions.explanation: Habeas tests custody. It does not itself adjudicate a visa, asylum application, or residence benefit.

questions.prompt: A judge orders a bond hearing. What can the advocate accurately tell the family?
options: The person has obtained a hearing; its outcome and the immigration case remain separate.
The removal case is over.
The person is guaranteed release.
questions.explanation: A hearing remedy supplies a process. The decision at that hearing and the immigration merits are distinct.

sections.title: 2. Choose the right legal vehicle
sections.subtitle: Habeas is a family of procedures, not one universal form.

parts.title: Federal custody and immigration detention
parts.text: Section 2241 authorizes specified custody challenges, including custody alleged to violate the Constitution, laws, or treaties of the United States. Immigration detention challenges commonly use this section. Custody is a legal requirement; present physical detention is the straightforward example, while other restraints and post-release cases require additional analysis. A volunteer’s role is to collect facts and identify urgency, not select and sign a petition as someone else’s lawyer.

parts.title: State convictions and federal sentences
parts.text: A person challenging custody under a state-court judgment generally proceeds under §2254, with its exhaustion and other restrictions. A federal prisoner attacking the validity of a federal sentence generally uses §2255 in the sentencing court, subject to its rules; its limited savings provision is not a free choice to use §2241 instead. State law may provide state habeas remedies too. This lesson’s district atlas addresses federal immigration detention, not a complete criminal postconviction guide.

parts.title: Separate the claims
parts.text: A challenge to the legal authority for confinement, a challenge to detention conditions, a challenge to a removal order, and a damages claim may require different vehicles and forums. Conditions claims are especially dependent on the requested relief and circuit law; do not assume every medical-care or facility complaint belongs in habeas. Counsel should classify each injury and requested remedy before combining claims.

questions.prompt: Which section is the usual starting point for a federal immigration-detention habeas petition?
options: 28 U.S.C. §2255 in every case
A state criminal appeal statute
questions.explanation: Immigration detention ordinarily uses §2241. The specific claim and jurisdiction still need review.

questions.prompt: A detained person also wants compensation for mistreatment. Best next step?
options: Omit the mistreatment from every record.
Assume a habeas petition automatically awards damages.
Separate custody, conditions, and damages issues for qualified legal review.
questions.explanation: Different injuries and remedies can require different causes of action and forums. Preserve the facts without promising a vehicle.

sections.title: 3. Find the court and custodian
sections.subtitle: Location is a legal fact, not a detail.

parts.title: The usual starting point
parts.text: For a core challenge to present physical custody, Rumsfeld v. Padilla supplies the default immediate-custodian and district-of-confinement rules. Start with the actual facility, its physical location, and the person who has day-to-day custody at the time of filing. The family’s home, counsel’s office, immigration court, ICE field office, and detention facility can be in different districts. Padilla expressly left an immigration-specific respondent question open; circuit law and particular facts must be checked rather than naming only a distant official by habit.

parts.title: Jurisdiction, venue, and transfer
parts.text: Subject-matter jurisdiction concerns the court’s authority over this kind of claim. Jurisdiction over the custodian and territorial limits concern whom the court can reach. Venue concerns the proper location for the case. These issues interact but are not interchangeable. Record transfers with precise dates and times. A transfer before filing may change the right court; a transfer after a properly filed petition raises preservation and respondent questions that counsel must analyze. Do not assume transfers always destroy—or always preserve—jurisdiction.

parts.title: Why D.C. is not a universal forum
parts.text: Naming federal officials in Washington does not make D.D.C. the right court for every detention case. In the Alien Enemies Act setting, Trump v. J.G.G. required the habeas challenge to be brought in the district of confinement and recognized notice and an opportunity to seek review before removal. That special statutory setting is distinct from ordinary INA removal-order review. Prompt qualified advice is crucial when transfer or removal is imminent.

questions.prompt: Luis lives in Missouri but is physically detained in Kansas. Where does core-custody forum analysis begin?
options: Automatically the district of his former Missouri home.
The district containing the Kansas detention facility.
Automatically Washington,D.C.
questions.explanation: Start with actual confinement and custodian, then examine governing circuit rules and any exception.

questions.prompt: ICE transfers a client before the petition is filed. What should the advocate do?
options: Confirm the new location and transfer timing immediately for counsel’s forum analysis.
Choose the immigration judge’s district automatically.
Use the old address without checking.
questions.explanation: The custody timeline can determine the proper forum and respondent.

sections.title: 4. Identify the detention statute
sections.subtitle: A custody challenge starts with the asserted source of power.

parts.title: Four common detention tracks
parts.text: Section 1225(b) concerns applicants for admission and specified inspection/expedited-removal situations; its mandatory-detention provisions and parole mechanisms require careful classification. Section 1226(a) supplies discretionary pre-decision custody and potential bond or conditional parole. Section 1226(c) requires detention for enumerated categories; current statutory text must be read, including amendments, rather than reduced to “any conviction.” Section 1231 governs detention after the relevant removal order and removal-period triggers. These are starting categories, not a substitute for analyzing the actual custody and removal record.

parts.title: Read the actual record
parts.text: Obtain custody notices, warrants, bond decisions, the Notice to Appear, entry and parole documents, criminal records, removal decisions, appeals, stays, and prior removal/reentry history. Ask what provision DHS asserts and whether the facts fit it. A pending appeal or judicial stay can affect the analysis; a reinstated order and withholding-only proceedings are a distinct configuration. Guzman Chavez held §1231 applicable to the reinstated-order withholding-only situation before it.

parts.title: The current interior-arrest dispute
parts.text: In2026 appellate courts disagree about using §1225(b)(2)(A) for people already living in the United States without admission who are arrested in the interior. Several circuits reject that classification on the facts before them; Fifth and Eighth Circuit opinions accept it. Even a §1226 classification does not guarantee bond eligibility or release: subsection(c), flight risk, dangerousness, and other applicable rules may matter. Use the atlas to begin regional research.

questions.prompt: Which information most helps counsel identify detention authority?
options: Custody papers plus entry, removal, appeal/stay, and relevant criminal records.
Only how long the family has lived here.
Only the person’s work card.
questions.explanation: The statute depends on procedural posture and facts; documents from several tracks may be necessary.

questions.prompt: A circuit says the petitioner falls under §1226 rather than §1225. Does that guarantee release?
options: Yes, if the person has a job.
Yes, automatically.
No; applicable mandatory categories and custody standards still require analysis.
questions.explanation: The statutory classification is one issue; bond eligibility and the custody outcome are additional issues.

sections.title: 5. Recognize a possible claim
sections.subtitle: Statutory authority and constitutional process are separate questions.

parts.title: Wrong authority or inadequate process
parts.text: A statutory claim may argue that DHS is using the wrong detention provision or exceeds its authority. A constitutional claim may challenge prolonged detention or inadequate individualized process under the applicable due-process framework. Those claims require different legal analyses. Section 1226(e) limits review of discretionary judgments, but it is not a universal bar to challenges to statutory authority or constitutional legality. A district judge is not simply a second immigration judge deciding the same bond factors anew.

parts.title: Do not turn six months into an automatic release date
parts.text: Zadvydas interpreted §1231(a)(6) to avoid indefinite post-removal-period detention: six months is a presumptively reasonable period; after that, the person must give good reason to believe removal is not significantly likely in the reasonably foreseeable future, and the government must respond with sufficient evidence. Six months alone does not establish release. Jennings rejected reading automatic periodic six-month hearings into §§1225(b),1226(a),and1226(c), while leaving constitutional issues for further consideration. Arteaga-Martinez rejected a statutory six-month hearing requirement under §1231(a)(6); constitutional arguments remained distinct.

parts.title: Build evidence for the actual theory
parts.text: Preserve detention dates, reasons for delay, prior custody decisions, access to counsel, health concerns, the government’s removal efforts, relevant country/travel-document information, and the person’s goals. An advocate should record what is known and unknown without coaching or inventing facts. Exhaustion may be a judicially imposed requirement in §2241 detention litigation, with exceptions that vary; neither “always exhaust everything” nor “never exhaust” is reliable national instruction. Counsel must check the circuit and the particular administrative remedy.

questions.prompt: A person has spent six months in detention. What can you conclude nationally?
options: Identify the statute and facts; six months is not a universal release or hearing rule.
They must be released tomorrow.
Every constitutional challenge is barred.
questions.explanation: Zadvydas, Jennings, and Arteaga-Martinez address different statutes and questions.

questions.prompt: What is the sound national advice about exhausting custody remedies before §2241?
options: Always wait indefinitely regardless of urgency.
Check the applicable circuit’s requirement, available remedy, and recognized exceptions with counsel.
Never pursue an administrative remedy.
questions.explanation: Exhaustion in immigration detention habeas must be researched for the claim, forum, and urgency.

sections.title: 6. Respect the limits on review
sections.subtitle: A detention petition is not a universal appeal from removal.

parts.title: The INA’s review channels
parts.text: Section 1252(a)(5) generally makes a petition for review in the appropriate court of appeals the exclusive route for judicial review of a removal order. Sections1252(b)(9),1252(g),and the expedited-removal limitations can create further jurisdiction disputes. A genuine custody claim may be different from a disguised attack on removal, but courts disagree about some claims’ relationship to removal proceedings. Read the exact allegations and remedy—not merely the label “habeas.”

parts.title: Expedited removal and special settings
parts.text: Thuraissigiam rejected the attempted use of habeas in the setting before it to obtain additional asylum review rather than release from custody. Do not use that holding as a statement that every detention challenge is unavailable, or treat habeas as a routine appeal from a negative fear determination. Alien Enemies Act cases involve a different statute and urgent judicial-review questions. The jurisdiction and notice holdings of J.G.G. do not establish the merits of every AEA challenge.

parts.title: Individual relief and class limits
parts.text: Aleman Gonzalez interpreted §1252(f)(1) to restrict lower courts’ classwide injunctions against operation of covered INA provisions, while the statute has an individual-application exception. Do not infer from an individual victory that a nationwide injunction or an identical remedy for every detainee follows. Existing class orders require examination of class definition, jurisdiction, geographic scope, appeals, stays, and the relief actually in effect.

questions.prompt: Someone wants a district judge to reverse a final removal order by renaming the filing “detention habeas.” What matters?
options: Whether the family prefers the district judge.
The caption alone.
The claim’s substance, requested remedy, and applicable §1252 review channels.
questions.explanation: Labels do not defeat jurisdictional limits. Removal-order review and custody review must be distinguished.

questions.prompt: An individual petitioner receives relief. Can an advocate announce that every detainee nationwide has the same order?
options: No; read the remedy, party/class scope, and current status.
Yes, if the case is shared online.
Yes, every individual judgment is nationwide.
questions.explanation: Scope and jurisdictional limits matter. Individual relief is not automatically classwide relief.

sections.title: 7. Prepare a useful handoff
sections.subtitle: Accuracy and urgency belong in the same file.

parts.title: A practical advocate checklist
parts.text: Confirm current custody location and safe communication; obtain informed permission to share records; record language and interpretation needs; create a dated custody and removal timeline; preserve actual notices and decisions; identify pending deadlines and possible imminent transfer/removal; document health and access concerns; connect the person to counsel qualified for the immigration and federal-court issues. Do not upload client details into this lesson. The learning tools store only quiz progress.

parts.title: What counsel must settle before filing
parts.text: Counsel needs the claim, statutory and constitutional grounds, proper petition verification and petitioner/representative authority, respondent, district, exhaustion analysis, supporting evidence, requested remedy, local admission and filing rules, applicable form/fee or financial application, service process, redaction/sealing requirements, emergency-motion procedure, and current case status. AO242 is a national §2241 form; verify whether the selected court requires its own form or different instructions. A family relationship alone does not automatically qualify someone to litigate as next friend.

parts.title: Emergency relief is a separate request
parts.text: Filing a habeas petition does not automatically stay removal or transfer. Counsel must analyze jurisdiction for the specific requested interim relief and use the applicable emergency procedure, with evidence of urgency and required notice/service. Section 2243 directs prompt action, but judicial scheduling and local orders determine actual response obligations; do not promise a hearing or release in a universal number of days. Preserve the court’s order and explain the next step accurately.

questions.prompt: A petition has been filed. Is removal automatically stayed?
options: Only because an advocate says it is.
No; counsel must analyze and obtain appropriate relief where authorized.
Yes.
questions.explanation: A filing is not itself a court order preventing removal or transfer.

questions.prompt: What belongs in the first federal-court handoff?
options: A verified timeline, actual custody/removal papers, urgent events, client goals, and open questions.
A guaranteed outcome.
An invented detention reason to strengthen the petition.
questions.explanation: A truthful, organized record supports qualified counsel’s analysis and preserves the person’s voice.

sections.title: 8. Read the district primer and recheck it
sections.subtitle: Today’s orientation is tomorrow’s research starting point.

parts.title: The current Supreme Court posture
parts.text: On October 1, 2026 the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, No. 26-104, concerning mandatory detention under §1225(b)(2)(A) of people present without admission. The grant is not a merits decision, not an automatic stay of all lower-court decisions, and not an instruction that everyone receives or loses bond. This edition’s cutoff is October 7, 2026 in America/Chicago. Review later orders and the docket before relying on the circuit map.

parts.title: A decision can stop being a usable rule
parts.text: A panel opinion may be reheard, vacated, stayed, narrowed, or superseded. In the Fifth Circuit, the July 2, 2026 Sosnava Rodriguez panel’s constitutional 90-day hearing rule was vacated July 10 for en banc review; do not teach it as binding law. A certiorari petition is an advocate’s filing, not a Supreme Court holding. A judge-specific standing order is not automatically a districtwide rule. The atlas identifies these differences and records research limits.

parts.title: How the 94-district atlas works
parts.text: Each entry identifies the regional circuit, linked appellate starting points, the official court, a local-filing checklist, and any independently verified local order or illustration found in this research. Shared circuit authority applies across its districts within the holding’s scope. A district decision is ordinarily persuasive rather than circuit precedent; binding class/injunction scope is a separate question. Where no local order was verified, the entry says so—it does not mean none exists. This is a dated orientation, not an exhaustive live PACER or citator survey.

parts.title: The update routine
parts.text: Before using a primer in a case, confirm physical custody and district; pull the cited opinion and latest docket; check publication, mandate, rehearing, vacatur and stays; check Supreme Court orders; examine the selected court’s latest local/general/judge orders; determine class membership and operative remedy; compare the actual detention statute and facts; record the date, sources, uncertainties, and counsel’s conclusion. The atlas does not monitor changes automatically. Independent immigration-practitioner review of this educational edition remains pending.

questions.prompt: The Supreme Court grants certiorari. What does that establish?
options: All detention ends.
The lower judgment is automatically reversed.
The Court agreed to review the case; merits and any stay must be checked separately.
questions.explanation: The October 1 order grants review. It does not itself resolve the statutory merits.

questions.prompt: A July panel opinion was vacated for en banc review. How should you use it?
options: Ignore all later orders.
Identify the vacatur and research the operative law and current docket.
As settled binding law.
questions.explanation: Status checking is part of accurate legal analysis. A vacated panel rule is not current binding precedent.

final.prompt: Luis is detained after a transfer. What comes first?
options: Select the court nearest his family automatically.
Promise release.
Locate him and record transfer timing and custody papers.
final.explanation: Location and timing ground the custodian, forum, and urgency analysis.

final.prompt: DHS cites §1225; Luis has lived in the interior for years without admission. Which inquiry is essential?
options: Whether the governing circuit’s current cases and his precise facts support that classification, including later Supreme Court action.
Whether a cousin once won a case.
Only whether he has a job.
final.explanation: The2026 statutory split must be checked against geography, facts, and current case status.

final.prompt: The family requests a guarantee because another detainee won. Best response?
options: The other judgment is irrelevant in every way.
Review its holding, scope, status, statute, and facts; explain that relief is not guaranteed.
Same result guaranteed.
final.explanation: A useful precedent must match the issue and remain legally usable.

final.prompt: A detained person has a final removal order and no foreseeable removal. What should counsel examine?
options: A new visa application alone.
The §1231 posture, Zadvydas framework, evidence, and current regional law.
Automatic release exactly six months after arrest in every case.
final.explanation: Post-removal-period analysis differs from pre-decision detention; six months is not an automatic release date.

final.prompt: You find an October 2 local standing order that amended an earlier hearing schedule. Which schedule should you report?
options: The older schedule because it appears in a template.
The operative amended order and any later case-specific order after checking scope/status.
A nationwide deadline invented from another district.
final.explanation: Local procedures and case-specific orders change; read the operative text.

final.prompt: What does completing this lesson authorize?
options: A learning record only; qualified counsel and current local requirements remain necessary.
CLE credit automatically.
Federal representation in every district.
final.explanation: The lesson supplies orientation, not professional authorization or accreditation.

circuits.label: Interior classification rejected on reviewed facts
circuits.holding: Guerrero Orellana v. Moniz (August 13, 2026) rejected §1225(b)(2)(A) for the long-present interior entrant in the case and upheld §1226(a) relief. Do not extend the holding to every border-arrival or §1226(c) case.
circuits.practice: Hernandez-Lara v. Lyons addresses §1226(a) hearing burdens: government proof of danger by clear-and-convincing evidence or flight risk by a preponderance. Reid v. Donelan rejects a categorical six-month §1226(c) hearing rule. Both require attention to their scope and later authority.

circuits.title: Second Circuit
circuits.label: Interior classification rejected; Supreme Court review pending
circuits.holding: Barbosa da Cunha v. Freden (April 28, 2026) treated the long-present interior entrant as detained under §1226(a), rather than §1225(b)(2)(A). Supreme Court review was granted October 1 in Rhoney, No. 26-104; no merits ruling is recorded at this cutoff.

circuits.title: Third Circuit
circuits.label: Interior classification rejected; removal-linked claim limits matter
circuits.holding: Buele Morocho v. Warden Philadelphia FDC (August 28, 2026) upheld relief for the interior detainees on the reviewed facts. Section 1226(c) did not apply to those petitioners. Do not equate that outcome with release for every detainee.

President United States (January 15, 2026) applied §1252(b)(9) to the removal-linked claims before it, while distinguishing detention-specific length or conditions issues. German Santos v. Warden Pike County uses a fact-dependent unreasonable-§1226(c)-detention inquiry rather than a universal bright line.

circuits.title: Fourth Circuit
circuits.label: Interior classification rejected; forum exceptions are factual
circuits.holding: Lopez Garcia v. Guadian (September 10, 2026) rejected §1225(b)(2)(A) for the long-present interior detainees before the court. Section 1226(a) permits a custody hearing opportunity; it does not guarantee release.
circuits.practice: Miranda v. Garland rejected a constitutional challenge to the initial §1226(a) hearing’s allocation of burden to the noncitizen. Suri v. Trump (July 23, 2026) recognized jurisdiction over its detention-specific claims and an exceptional concealed-location/transfer forum scenario. Trump v. Suri, No. 26-380, is a pending Supreme Court petition at this cutoff; the exception is not general permission to file where family lives.

circuits.label: Interior classification accepted; vacated hearing rule

Underlying judgments were stayed July 21; en banc argument occurred September 24. Do not teach 90 days as the current rule. Check the en banc docket and the pending Supreme Court statutory dispute before using earlier templates.

circuits.label: Interior classification rejected on reviewed facts
circuits.holding: Lopez-Campos v. Raycraft (May 11, 2026) rejected the broad §1225(b)(2) approach for the interior residents before it and upheld hearing relief under §1226. It does not create blanket eligibility for mandatory-§1226(c) detainees or border arrivals.

circuits.holding: Avila v. Bondi (March 25, 2026) adopted the §1225(b)(2)(A) statutory interpretation for the unadmitted interior petitioner and reversed a Minnesota hearing grant. This differs from the Tenth Circuit approach relevant in Kansas.
circuits.practice: Counsel must separate the adverse classification holding from any distinct constitutional, prolonged-detention, post-removal-period, or other claim. Do not assume Missouri follows Kansas. Check later rehearing, mandate, stay, and Supreme Court action.

circuits.label: Interior classification rejected; distinct expedited-removal claim
circuits.holding: Rodriguez Vazquez v. Bostock (July 30, 2026) rejected the broad interior §1225(b)(2) interpretation in the reviewed class case. Section 1226(c) and ordinary danger/flight considerations still matter. Review class membership, actual operative relief, and later stays.

It was an interlocutory jurisdiction ruling, not a final holding that all §1225 detainees are entitled to bond. Do not confuse this Padilla case with Rumsfeld v. Padilla.

circuits.label: Interior classification rejected on reviewed facts
circuits.holding: Santillan Quiroz v. Mullin (June 30, 2026) rejected §1225(b)(2)(A) for the long-present interior arrestee and directed a bond hearing or release on the case’s terms. That case-specific seven-day remedy is not a nationwide filing or hearing deadline.
circuits.practice: Kansas follows this regional authority within its scope; Missouri is in the Eighth Circuit. Detention location can therefore change the governing appellate starting point. Identify §1226(c), final-order or other distinct posture, and current docket status before predicting a remedy.
